content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper attempts to improve on existing pretraining and input strategies for developing multimodal deep representations. The authors introduce a novel multi-modal token "embedding" as a way towards reducing the complexity of the model as well as a simple but effective approach towards task sampling to leverage various datasets in the VQA domain. The result is improvements in the state of the art for models trained with the proposed approach at the pretraining dataset range the authors explored.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The main strenght is the straightforward nature of the main contribution. The proposed "Joint adaptive representation" unifies the 2 domains into a single representation in 3 steps. The image tokenization is queried from the image in the style of TokenLearner, and then a cross-attention mechanism is applied to learn a unified representation across the modes. This cross-attention is applied iteratively: to fuse both the image and text modes as well as the new multi-modal representation. A small number of iterations is applied in this fashion (between 1 and 8). This is a novel architecture for feature fusion that has computational and accuracy benefits clearly outlined in the paper.

A key weakness is the perf analysis relies on the use of GFlops. GFlops often serves as a poor surrogate for runtime, especially when complex sequences of references to memory are used in large channel/hidden dimension domains. This can result in a lot of added memory access cost which results in the runtime not following the suggested pattern from the GFlops. I cannot tell from this paper whether such a cost would be incurred, but the authors could do an ablation to understand this better. I understand that doing runtime analysis on a large set of architectures is not practical, but if a primary claim of the paper is a more efficient model then I think some time comparisons should be done. If not, then other benefits that can be derived from the lower GFlops cost should be highlighted and explored.

Another weakness is the lack of any qualitative analysis in the paper. Specifically, the claim "by adap- tively tokenizing the inputs, the model is able to select the best information for use across modali- ties" seems hard to corroborate quantitatively, and the authors should at least provide some anecdotal evidence.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is written very clearly and provides a reasonable empirical analysis to support the claims made in the paper. The approach is novel to the best of my knowledge. The authors plan to open source the code.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is a simple but effective improvement on a commonly used multimodal learning architecture. The method is explained clearly and empirical evidence for the usefulness is good. While there are some limitations in the performance analysis (GFlops does not account for memory cost in the proposed feature multimodal fusion modules) this does not detract from the paper significantly. Some qualitative analysis would also benefit the paper.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3212 by Reviewer jk3m

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for the review. We agree fully that FLOPs is a lacking measurement for model performance, as it can hide issues with memory, runtime, etc. However, comparing runtime is quite difficult as no previous works report it, and there are differences in implementations (PyTorch vs. Tensorflow vs. JAX) and hardware (TPUs vs. GPUs), all which can influence the runtime, depending on how the model is built and compiled. 

We will note that in addition to reducing FLOPs, we also saw a reduction in memory usage during training and inference. For a training batch, the memory was reduced from 15gb to 9gb comparing the concat baseline to our approach.

We can add some runtime comparisons to the various baselines we implemented for the ablations (Table 2), and we could compare runtimes to some previous work, but due to implementation differences, it may be hard to attribute the differences to approach or implementation.

We agree with the reviewer that the "by adaptively tokenizing the inputs…” statement, as pointed out by the reviewer, is unsubstantiated (it reflects an intuition only). So we have revised it appropriately.

We will add some more visualizations to the appendix, thanks for the great suggestions.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3212 by Reviewer agT4

content.title: Response
content.comment:
We would like to engage the reviewer in discussions as soon as possible, because we find the comments are lacking in explanation and justification or are inadmissible or inaccurate. Thank you.


1.Lock of novelty.

We believe this is incorrect, and other reviewers (e.g. jk3m) highlight the novelty in the approach. Our innovations provide improvements to existing methods that greatly reduce compute cost and increase accuracy, and allow for our model (trained only on public and well understood data) to outperform much larger and more expensive algorithms (some trained on large and private datasets).

2.The reviewer thought the result in this paper was not very satisfactory. Not SOTA performance and VQAv2 SOTA is 84+ for now.

We believe this argument is not valid. There has been recent work which to our knowledge has not been published at the time of submission.   

3.This article is very terribly written, perhaps with the intention of fooling the reviewers? For example, the authors claim that they propose a method to reduce flops, but in Table 2(a) of ablation, we can see that Method-Add and Method-Ours_gated have the same flops.


We believe this statement is invalid as well. Table 2(a) first two rows clearly shows decrease in GFLOPs from 54 to 38 GFLOPs for the small sized models,  Table 2(a), last two lines is just an ablation (within our own approach, e.g., on the effect of \alpha and \beta in Eq. 3) which compares versions of our approach, concluding that using gating is helpful. Gating adds no FLOPs which is why they are the same in FLOPs.  Table 5 clearly shows our method has 38 and 54 GFLOPs for the small and large models, whereas most others are 100-300 (or even 900) GFLOPs. Table 1 clearly compares the reduction in FLOPs and gain in accuracy with respect to the main competitive approaches in a direct side-by-side comparison.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes some changes for V&L models like ALBEF that combine the vision and the language representations during the encoding phase. The observation is that fusing through concatenation of tokens is expensive, and cross attention into the language is sub-optimal due to the low number of tokens representing the language information. So the authors propose an alternative in which a number of tokens that are not associated to either stream but rather serve the purpose of fusing the information. This is similar to prior work such as perceiver but the details make it more efficient. Some other modifications, like gating of residual connections and some adaptive adjustment of the tasks/losses used for training complete the set of improvements. The evaluation is exclusively on VQA.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
The topic of vision and language is of high relevance, and the specific problem of how to train models with more modest resources is very relevant too. 
The models the authors compare against are state-of-the-art on a core problem. In fact, many of the papers are very recent 2022 papers. 
The proposed changes seem to have a positive impact on performance and the proposed method compares positively in terms of accuracy vs cost. 

Cons:
* The methodological improvements are incremental. The authors propose to tweak 3 components, each adding a little bit of performance. The fusion mechanism, which is the more methodologically relevant of the 3 improvements, resembles previous mechanisms (perceiver).
* Narrow validation, including 2 VQA and a visual entailment dataset. ALBEF validates on a large number of tasks (2 vs 5) and datasets (3 vs 5). 
* Ablations on same number of images as other methods would be very useful too. I know this is an issue in the literature, but each paper in Table 5 has a different training set. This obviously makes comparisons very hard. The authors could use some method (e.g. ALBEF) and show performance on the same training set for a more direct comparison.
* Clarity of exposition is lacking. See below for details.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The text is clearly written and the explanations are rather easy to understand. However, the paper includes a lot of text explanations on methodological similarities and differences. Explaining these concepts only in natural language is clearly sub-optimal when you can write down the methodologies formally and the result is much more precise and clear. Unfortunately the explanations are also repeated in several places, leading to a verbose paper. The methodological details only cover the proposed method, but how it compares or extends prior work is not clearly defined. The two alternative fusion methods are not laid out beyond verbal descriptions, and the differences with perceiver and co-tokenizer are only verbally described. No graphical abstract is given either, and no visual comparison of architectures is included. Instead, Fig.1 and Fig.2 use quite a bit of space but do not add clarity as a graphical abstract would, see e.g. Fig. 1 in ALBEF paper (but maybe in this case also add comparison with alternative methods) or Fig. 2 on METER. 
Just to be very clear: the intuition behind the formulation in textual form is very important and needs to be included, but this has to be combined with a formal description (not substituted by a formal description). 

Quality: I appreciate the challenge of beating the very last V&L models - this is actually one of the big pluses. The technical challenge is not trivial.

Novelty: the paper is mostly incremental, even though one can argue that simple is better if the performance return is solid. Maybe some better validation could be done to support this argument.

Reproducibility: Authors claim that the code will be released. The paper is not straightforward to reproduce, but is not particularly obscure either. Some parameters are given in the appendix.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed method is a bit incremental, but it is also tackling an important problem and competing with very recent and well-performing works. So overall, the paper has the potential, but it is a bit lacking in terms of width of the evaluation (more tasks/datasets would be great) and clarity of exposition (much more formal description and less verbose explanations).
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

Thank you for your suggestions for improvements.

We agree our method is based on previous influential approaches (Perceiver and Co-Tokenization, the latter borrowed from video understanding). We have clearly stated this connection throughout the paper and also demonstrate in Table 2 how we are able to outperform both and do so with fewer FLOPs.  This translates to a lot of GLOPs savings for image-language learning, and leads to a small but powerful model, which we hope to offer with this contribution.

Validation on more datasets & more ablations: We will try to include more datasets and ablations as recommended. We will add the results using the same data as ALBEF to the table. We will try to include them by the end of the rebuttal period.
 
Clarity: Thank you for these suggestions, incl. recommendations for a figure and clarifications, we have updated the paper and will continue to improve it. We have added a new Fig 1 visually comparing our approach to others.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method for learning joint vision and language representations. Using transformer backbones for both modalities, a straightforward for this purpose involves applying cross attention between the two modalities. To cope with the computational overhead caused by a large number of tokens(specifically visual tokens), the authors propose to reduce the number of tokens via sampling.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- The problem set-up is an active line of research.
- The main idea of the paper is simple.

Weaknesses:

- Presentation:
 Unfortunately, the writing quality of this paper does not match ICLR standards. My main question lies in Eq (2). How $X_N$ is precisely learned? What is a function that generates $X_N$, what are its inputs, and what is the objective function that it is optimizing? The paper just says that $X_N$ is learned in a DETR-style, which is very wage. Here is a list of minor points in this regard. It would be better to include a figure that explains the method. Figure 1. and referring to it in the introduction are not informative. 2) I did not find the writing accurate in general. For instance, Section 3 starts with a paragraph of two lines. The second paragraph starts with a preposition and is not well organized. In the third paragraph, the authors mention that "These few tokens put great pressure on the cross-attention later". What does "pressure" mean precisely? 3) Eq(1) and the corresponding paragraph are obvious and unnecessary. 

- Contribution :
I could not understand the contribution of this paper precisely. Is it about learning $X_N$? If so, how is it done precisely? 

- Performance:
The paper underperforms some recent approaches. More specifically, BLIP[1] tackles the same problem and archives higher performance.

[1] Li etal, BLIP: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training for Unified Vision-Language Understanding and Generation
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Unfortunately, I do not believe at this stage that the paper matches ICLR standards in terms of clarity, quality, and novelty. I'd be happy to discuss this with the authors. Please see the weaknesses for more detailed feedback.
content.summary_of_the_review: The above-mentioned weaknesses prevent me from leaning towards accepting this paper. I believe the presentation is not clear, the contributions are marginal, and the performance paper is not satisfactory.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for the comments and suggestions. We welcome further discussion and comments, please take a look at our responses especially with regards to BLIP and contributions.	

**X_N**: Thank you, we have improved the clarity with respect to learning X_N. X_N is part of the representation being learned (as an intermediate projection) and while a bit unintuitive, as is DETR itself, this feature representation is learned from the overall loss of the (end-to-end) image-language learning system. We have further  improved the writing, joined the paragraphs and rephrased the issues pointed out (added in the revised version). Please let us know if it addressed your concerns.

**Contributions**: Our contribution goes beyond learning X_N, we provide a novel joint representation learning (from both modalities, Eqns. 3 & 4) and joint-pretraining which produces much smaller (and accurate) models with fewer FLOPS, using smaller datasets. Our model outperforms other much larger & more powerful models. We believe this will be a very valuable contribution for many who do not have large training resources or datasets.

**BLIP**: We disagree with the reviewer stating that our approach underperforms BLIP. Two versions of BLIP are added very clearly in the main Table (Table 5), where we see that our approach outperforms both of them, with our small model too, and has 3 times or 6 times fewer flops.
